newsitem.title: CANADA: RBC Dominion seen grabbing rival Richardson soon.
newsitem.headline: RBC Dominion seen grabbing rival Richardson soon.

text.p: Royal Bank of Canada's RBC Dominion Securities Inc is on the brink of acquiring Richardson Greenshields, one of Canada's last independent brokerages, industry sources said on Thursday.
The takeover of its main rival would help RBC Dominion reclaim its crown as Canada's largest brokerage.
"It's a done deal. It's either going to be today or early tomorrow," said one observer who declined to be identified.

He said the takeover would be done at around C$450 million, or roughly twice the book value of Richardson Greenshields which is 70 percent-owned by the Richardson family of Winnipeg. The remaining 30 percent is held by employees.

RBC Dominion lost its title as Canada's biggest broker when Bank of Montreal's Nesbitt Thomson stole it in 1994 with the acquisition of Burns Fry Inc. The resulting behemoth with a retail sales staff of 1,268 was named Nesbitt Burns Inc.
Traders and analysts predicted the focus will now shift to Midland Walwyn Inc, the last bachelor in the industry with a substantial sales staff. Midland employs more than 1,000 sales people.

"It would appear that RBC are adding distribution, that is to say, an additional 500 retail salespeople to raise the ante again on Bay Street," said Jim Doak, director and vice-president of investment research.
"This will swing the focus onto Midland Walwyn which is the last independent broker with a large retail sales force."
Officials at Richardson and RBC Dominion were unavailable for comment. Royal Bank's shares eased 0.05 to 34.70
Midland shares rose 0.80 on Wednesday and another 0.80 late morning on Thursday to trade at 9.65 as speculation grew that the powerful Canadian banks may look to it as the next desirable target.
One trader said there is speculation that ScotiaMcLeod Inc, the brokerage arm of Bank of Nova Scotia, could bid for Midland.
--Sarah Edmonds, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100, E-mail sarah.edmonds@reuters.com
